food.text: During the early modern period, European merchant and slave ships brought chili peppers, maize and tomatoes from the New World to West Africa. These crops have since become ubiquitous parts of West African cooking.
West Africa had its own native spices, including grains of paradise, grains of Selim, alligator pepper and calabash nutmeg. Some of these were traded to Europeans, who sought them out.

Portuguese presence on the Gold Coast brought American crops such as maize and cassava into African farming. Sugar, guava, sweet potatoes, coconut and yams also joined the agricultural landscape, which globalized the region's farming and output.
West African ingredients crossed the Atlantic as well. Slave ships carried black-eyed peas, West African rice, roselle, ackee, garden egg, palm oil and okra to the New World.

The traditional West African way to prepare cassava is to peel the roots and soak them in water for three days to ferment. They are then dried or cooked, and in Nigeria and several other countries they are often grated and lightly fried in palm oil to make garri. Fermenting also lowers the level of antinutrients, making the cassava more nutritious.

At the time of Columbus's arrival in the New World, the Portuguese traded from the Gulf of Guinea for grains of paradise, an African spice then best known as melegueta pepper, as a substitute for Asian black pepper. African slaves loved the grains of paradise already familiar in their culture, but they were fascinated by the fiery Capsicum pepper. The local chilis were named malagueta because their piquancy was reminiscent of Old World pepper.

The Songhai ruler Sonni Ali had several dikes built during his reign. These enhanced the irrigation and agricultural yield of the empire, whose wealth came mainly from overland Sahel trade and river trade along the Niger.

Historian James C. McCann argued that jollof rice spread with the Mali Empire, carried by Djula tradespeople who took rice agronomy, small-scale marketing and blacksmithing to regional centers. Fran Osseo-Asare traces the dish to the Jolof area of Senegal, where the original thieboudienne held rice, fish, shellfish and vegetables.
Timbuktu flourished on the trade in salt, gold and ivory. After the Moroccan conquest of 1591, its trade declined in part because of competition from newly available trans-Atlantic sailing routes.

Kola nuts were particularly useful on slave ships to improve the taste of water, because enslaved Africans were often given poor quality water to drink. A French voyager named Chevalier Des Marchais, who traveled to West Africa in the late 1720s, noted that the nut made the "bitterest, our sourest Things taste Sweet after it." The article attributes this sweetening to chemical substances the nut adds to the palate, or to the sheer amount of caffeine.

Around 1550, the Mali Empire reinforced its hold on trade routes bringing gold and kola nuts to and from the Akan states and the European trading post at Elmina. Kola nuts were thus a valued trade good alongside gold.

In the past, West Africans ate much less meat and cooked with native oils: palm oil on the coast and shea butter in Sahelian regions. Baobab leaf and many local greens were everyday staples at certain times of the year.

art.text: The Sankoré Mosque in Timbuktu was established in the 14th-15th centuries and rebuilt in the 16th century, with later additions. It had a tapering minaret and a prayer hall with rows of arches, and it is a prime example of Sudano-Sahelian architecture.

The Bamana people adapted many artistic traditions, including pottery, sculpture, weaving, iron figures and masks. Most of these traditions were part of sacred vocations, created as a display of religious beliefs and used in ritual. A Bamana Empire rose in the 1740s.

Under Songhai influence, minarets took on a more pyramidal appearance and became stepped or tiered on three levels. The tower of the mosque-tomb of Askia al-Hajj Muhammad in Gao, in present-day Mali, is the example given.

Bamana artworks were created both for religious use and to define cultural and religious difference. This mattered because the Bamana state practised and formalised traditional polytheistic religion, in contrast to its Muslim neighbors.
Osei Tutu, with help from Okomfo Anokye, unified what became the Ashante into a confederation. The Golden Stool served as a symbol of their unity and spirit. His reign is dated c. 1695 to 1717.

The economy of the Ghanaian kingdom grew through trade in gold, cloth, and enslaved people, and this wealth supported the development of its artistic culture. Ghanaian artworks range from wood carvings to brass works, figures, and gems.

Western architecture has influenced the coastal areas of Africa since the late 15th century. Evidence suggests African architecture in some areas had already been shaped by external cultures for centuries before that.

The tapering minarets of Timbuktu's Sankoré Mosque may reflect cultural contacts with the M'zab region to the north. Its decoration may reflect contacts with Berber communities in what is now Mauritania. Local pagan cultures may also have influenced later Islamic architecture in the region.

war.text: In 1591 Songhai forces under Emperor Askia Ishaq II met a Saadi army led by Judar Pasha at the Battle of Tondibi. Despite vastly superior numbers, the Songhai were routed by a cattle stampede triggered by the Saadi's gunpowder weapons. Judar then sacked Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné, destroying the Songhai as a regional power.

In 1690s Ghana, the Komenda Wars, fought from 1694 until 1700, pitted the Dutch West India Company against the English Royal African Company in the Eguafo Kingdom over trade rights. Many African forces joined in, and historian John Thornton called it a fine example of European rivalry merging with African rivalry. The fighting included a civil war in Eguafo, and in November 1698 an English-led attack killed the Eguafo king Takyi. The wars and a smallpox outbreak in the early 1700s led to significant depopulation of the coastal area.

In 1712 Mamari Kulubali, also known as Biton Coulibaly, reorganized a youth organization called a tòn into a personal army supplemented with runaway slaves. He fortified Ségou with Songhai techniques and built a large army of conscripts, the ton djon, plus a navy of war canoes to patrol the Niger.

In 1591 at the Battle of Tondibi, Judar Pasha's Saadi army faced Askia Ishaq II's much larger Songhai force. The Songhai were routed by a cattle stampede triggered by the Saadi's gunpowder weapons, and Judar then sacked Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné.

Judar Pasha was a Spaniard by birth but had been captured as an infant and educated at the Saadi court. After a march across the Sahara desert, his forces captured, plundered and razed the salt mines at Taghaza before moving on to Gao.

From 1500 to 1510, Askia Muhammad's forces picked apart Mali's remaining provinces in the Sahel. In 1506 he raided Galam on the Senegal river, wiping away the last vestiges of Mali's rule in the Sahel, though Songhai did not permanently occupy the Senegal.
war.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

war.text: After the Songhai were destroyed by a Moroccan invasion in 1593, Mansa Mahmud IV saw a chance to restore Malian pre-eminence in the Niger bend. Outside Jenne in 1599, the Moroccans beat his army thanks to their firearms and to the betrayal of Bukar of Kala, a vassal who secretly went over to them. The Malian army was scattered, though Mahmud was able to escape, and the defeat crippled his prestige. Bambara and Fula war bands then marauded through the countryside and eventually sacked Niani, and when Mahmud died in 1610 his sons fought over the throne and the empire splintered.

The last Komenda war began in November 1699 with a unified force supporting Takyi Kuma. Panyarring, the seizing of members of rival forces, became a large-scale process between the different groups and heightened tensions. In early 1700, merchants associated with Twifo and John Cabess were panyarred by Adom, possibly on the instructions of the Dutch, and violence stayed sporadic until a British-supported mercenary force moved upon Eguafo. On May 9, 1700, Takyi Kuma was named the new king of Eguafo, and the English had placed their candidate in power.

Around 1550, a Malian force attacked Bighu to reinforce the empire's hold over the trade routes carrying gold and kola nuts. These routes ran to and from the Akan states and the European trading post at Elmina.

In 1512 Tengela invaded Diara, and its people called on Songhai rather than Mali for defense, showing how much prestige the mansa had lost. Songhai sent an expedition under Kurmina-fari Umar Komdiagla, a brother of Askia Muhammad. Tengela was defeated and killed, ending the Tengela War.
war.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

war.text: Bitòn Coulibaly defeated an invasion from the Kong Empire in 1725, which cemented his position. He then attacked the Fulani, the Soninke and the Mossi, conquering Macina, Beledougou, Djenne, Bamako and Tomboctou, though he held the latter only briefly. In 1751 he conquered Niani, making the Mansa of Mali a vassal.

In 1590 Al-Mansur took advantage of civil conflict in the Songhai Empire and sent an army under Judar Pasha to gain control of the trans-Saharan trade routes. The conflict followed a war of succession after Askia Daoud died in 1583, which had split the empire into two feuding factions.

Mali's army was split between a northern command under the Farima-Soura and a southern command under the Sankaran-Zouma. At the siege of Jenne in 1599, both refused to follow Mansa Mamadu to battle, and their refusal resulted in his failure.
war.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

war.text: War broke out in February 1695 when forces of the merchant John Cabess attacked the Dutch fort at Komenda and prevented reinforcements from reaching it. On April 28, 1695, the Twifo forces were defeated. Later that year, during negotiations, the Dutch head at the fort, Willem Bosman, drew a pistol on June 26 and tried to shoot Cabess. Much of the fighting was panyarring, in which one force regularly seized members of other groups, and panyarring and occasional violence continued until a short-lived peace at the end of 1695.

literature.text: The Songhai scholar Mahmud Kati (1468-1593) wrote the Tarikh al-fattash, a chronicle of his region. Like many Muslim accounts, it described Sonni Ali as a tyrant, showing how West African scholars shaped the memory of their rulers in writing.

The Islamic historian Al-Sa'di, another chronicler of the Songhai world, shared the view of Sonni Ali as a tyrant. He described Sonni Ali's incursion on Timbuktu: Sonni Ali entered the city, burned and destroyed the town, and brutally tortured many people there. Al-Sa'di wrote that the "Godless tyrant" slaughtered those who remained in Timbuktu and humiliated them.

Leo Africanus visited at the beginning of the 16th century, and his descriptions of the territorial domains of Mali showed that it was still a kingdom of considerable size. The Tarikh al-Sudan likewise records that Mali remained a sizeable state in the 15th century.

The Songhai scholar Mahmud Kati (1468-1593) authored the chronicle Tarikh al-fattash. He was among the Muslim writers who described the Songhai ruler Sonni Ali as a tyrant, after Sonni Ali's invasion of Timbuktu. In the account of the historian Al-Sa'di, Sonni Ali burned and destroyed the town, brutally tortured many people, and slaughtered those who remained.

science.text: A German who visited in 1603-1604 reported that people washed themselves three times a day and then anointed themselves with tallow or palm oil. He called palm oil "an excellent medicine". It protected the skin and hair as well as serving as a cosmetic.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: In West Africa, iron production centres in Banjeli and Bassar in Togo reached up to 80,000 cubic meters, more than production at places such as Meroe. Analyses indicate that fifteenth- and sixteenth-century slags there were bloomery waste products, while preliminary analyses of objects suggest low-carbon steels.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: Many Africans considered palm oil a medicine in its own right, and it also served as a medium for delivering other curative substances. Historical sources recount healers mixing herbs with palm oil to treat skin conditions or ease headaches.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: By 1679, Barbot observed that Takoradi in Ghana was a major canoe-producing center. Its workers crafted dugouts capable of carrying up to eight tons, and the Ahanta people had already been making canoes there in the 1590s.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: Foreign visitors praised the soap made from palm and palm kernel oils mixed with ashes from palm fronds. One writer attested that "the Negroes Cloathes are very clean". The roasting method used to extract kernel oil gave West African "black soap" its characteristic color.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: Komenda and Takoradi in Ghana were production areas for dugout canoes made by the Ahanta people in the 1590s. In the 1660s, Muller observed that the Fetu people had bought dugout canoes made by the Ahanta.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: André Thevet (1516-1590) received his information from informants on the West African coast in 1555. He made note of the physicians, hospitals and medicine within Mali, and in Timbuktu, then under the Songhai Empire. He recorded that the most common disease in the country was one called Borozaiu or Zail, which he said stemmed solely from sexual promiscuity, to which the people were highly prone. It affected the private parts of men and women, and was treated with various decoctions, particularly the herb Achanaca.
Between the 17th and 18th centuries, Shama was a production area and marketplace for dugout canoes. Later it became only a marketplace, on Supome Island.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

politics.text: In the 17th century, the area of present-day Ghana was a center for trade and cultural exchange. The states there were linked by trading networks and shared cultural beliefs but stayed politically independent. This lasted until the early 18th century, when Osei Tutu began a vast land expansion that unified them.

In 1591 the Songhai Empire, one of the largest African empires in history, collapsed after the Battle of Tondibi. A Saadi army under Judar Pasha met Emperor Askia Ishaq II there. Despite vastly superior numbers (according to one account, 30,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry), the Songhai forces were routed by a cattle stampede triggered by the Saadi's gunpowder weapons. The Saadi invaders had thousands of arquebusiers and eight English cannons.

In 1712 Mamari Kulubali, also known as Biton Coulibaly, was elected leader of a youth organization called a tòn. He turned it into a personal army supplemented with runaway slaves and took the title bitòn. He set about overthrowing the traditional political order and became the first Faama of Ségou, capital of a new Bamana Empire.

Osei Kofi Tutu I, with the help of Okomfo Anokye, unified the Ashante into a confederation with the Golden Stool as a symbol of their unity and spirit. He built up the Ashante army, turning a disciplined militia into an effective fighting machine. In 1701 the Ashante conquered Denkyira, giving them access to coastal trade with Europeans, especially the Dutch.

Judar Pasha, who led the Saadi conquest of the Songhai, was a Spaniard by birth. He had been captured as an infant and educated at the Saadi court. After crossing the Sahara, his forces captured, plundered, and razed the salt mines at Taghaza and moved on to Gao.

Bitòn Kulubali built a large army of conscripts known as the ton djon and a navy of war canoes to patrol the Niger. His state rested on slavery: the army was made up of forobadjon, nominally slaves of the community, led by tondjons, slaves of the ton who were in practice a military aristocracy. Slaves captured in the empire's many wars were traded, and the demand for them drove further fighting. His defeat of an invasion from the Kong Empire in 1725 cemented his position.

In 1544 or 1545, a Songhai force led by kanfari Dawud sacked the Malian capital and used the royal palace as a latrine during a brief occupation. In 1558 the Songhai imposed an onerous peace, pushing their control westward to the Sansanding and Segou areas. Askia Dawud also married the Mansa's daughter.

The Keita dynasty remained a major power in West Africa from the early 13th century until the breakup of the Mali Empire around 1610. Rivals from within the clan then founded smaller kingdoms within contemporary Mali and Guinea. These are sometimes called "daughter dynasties".
The Futa Jallon state, located mainly in present-day Guinea, governed itself under a written constitution. Rule alternated between two rival political parties, the Soriya and the Alphaya.

Judar Pasha sacked Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné, destroying the Songhai as a regional power. Governing so vast an empire proved too much for the Saadi dynasty. They soon relinquished control of the region, letting it splinter into dozens of smaller kingdoms.

Emperor Askia Daoud died in 1583, and a war of succession split the Songhai Empire into two feuding factions. Askia Ishaq II ascended to power in the long dynastic struggle that followed. In 1590 Al-Mansur took advantage of the civil conflict and sent an army against the Songhai.

In 1766, Ngolo Diarra, a former slave and leader of the ton djon, seized the throne of Ségou after years of instability and civil war. He re-established stability and reigned for nearly thirty years of prosperity. He began a series of conquests, including that of Timbuktu and the Sultanate of Massina. His death came in battle.

Mali Empire hopes of taking advantage of Songhai's collapse ended with a disastrous defeat outside Djenne in 1599. The empire then rapidly disintegrated and was replaced by independent chiefdoms. The Keitas retreated to the town of Kangaba, where they became provincial chiefs.

Portuguese traders at Elmina used cloth, linens, beads, copper and brass pots, pans and bracelets, and slaves as bartering tools to obtain gold from the native merchants of Elmina. The Portuguese imported slaves to Elmina throughout the sixteenth century, using them primarily to transport goods to and from interior African states, but also to exchange with local Elminans for gold. The main supply of Gold Coast slaves came from the trade route between Benin and Elmina, which also supplied the Portuguese with cotton, cloth and beads.

philosophy.text: From the early 16th century, migrating Adja peoples formed the basis of the emergent Fon people. They came to practice Vodún, a religion teaching a supreme creator divinity ruling over lesser spirits called vodúns, who were honored at shrines with offerings.
In 1725, Fula pastoralists in West Africa rose in armed revolt against indigenous chiefdoms. By 1750, they had founded the Imamate of Futa Jallon, placing the region under Islamic sharia law.

By the 1790s, the Islamic scholar Usman dan Fodio had become popular across the Hausa Kingdoms. He preached that Muslim rulers were obligated to govern ethically and generously, while openly condemning corruption, hypocrisy and the oppression of fellow Muslims.
Beginning in 1727, the Kingdom of Dahomey became a vassal state of the Yoruba-led Oyo Empire. During this period of religious exchange, the Fon adopted the Yoruba cults of Fá, Oró and Egúngún.
The Fá divination cult, adopted from the Yoruba, was present among the Fon people by the reign of Dahomey's king Tegbesu, who ruled from 1732 to 1774.

The Fon first made contact with Portuguese sailors in the 16th century, followed by French, British, Dutch and Danish traders in the 17th and 18th centuries. The earliest document recording European interest in Vodún was the Doctrina Christiana, dated 1658.
In 1725, Alpha Ibrahima Sambegu was elected as the first Almaamy, or religious-political ruler, of the Futa Jallon state. Its capital was Timbo, in present-day Guinea.

After the Moroccan invasion of 1591, Timbuktu's scholars had to flee or face imprisonment or murder. In 1593, many of the city's scholars were executed or exiled for disloyalty to the new rulers. This struck at a reputation built on the Sankoré Madrasah and an important book trade, and together with falling trade it cost the city its prominence.

By 1773, Usman dan Fodio had completed one of his most influential works, Ihya' al-sunna wa ikhmad al-bid'a (The Revival of the Prophetic Practice and Obliteration of False Innovation). The book established his reputation among contemporary Islamic scholars.

Usman dan Fodio once entered a scholarly dispute with local scholars over points of Islamic scholasticism. He responded by writing more than fifty separate works arguing against what he saw as their flawed reasoning.

culture.text: Christianity was largely introduced to West Africa from the late 18th century onward, when missionaries from European countries brought the religion to the region. In practice, elements of traditional African religion have mixed with Christianity.

The Bamana formed their own empire in 1640 and borrowed much from the Mali Empire, including the sofa, a slave soldier drawn from jonow (slaves) captured in battle or bought from afar. Jonow became part of their master's clan and were often freed after a certain number of years.

In the 16th century, warriors from the crumbling Mali Empire invaded what is now Sierra Leone and Liberia. They set up a loose federation of Mané states paying homage to a single leader, an empire that visiting Europeans called Kquoja. By the end of the 17th century, the Mané had conquered nearly all the indigenous cultures, which spread the Mandé language and ended the single Kquoja authority.

After Mamari's death in 1755, Dinkoro Coulibaly reigned for a few years before being overthrown by his brother Ali, and the list of Faamas records that the ton djon assassinated Dinkoro. Ali, a devout Muslim, attempted to convert the empire to Islam and was soon deposed himself by the ton djon.
The Mané conscripted conquered people into their armies as sumbas. The sumbas were forced to engage in ritual cannibalism, which permanently alienated them from the Mané ruling class.
